column4: 1.  **Precontemplation**: He sees himself as a *firm* but *loving* parent. He believes raising his voice is necessary. He’s not considering changing. In fact, he might even justify it- “That’s how my dad raised me.”

column4: Godly sorrow, or <u>the experience of sadness or distress that leads to a *metanoia*</u>, is not the same thing worldly sorrow. Worldly sorrow is the same experience of sadness or distress, but the world offers no hope, only the relief and promise of death.
column5: Godly sorrow, or <u>the experience of grief or distress that brings about *metanoia*</u>, is not the same as worldly sorrow. Worldly sorrow is the same experience of grief or distress, but the world offers no hope, only relief and the promise of death.

column4: Sorrow is also different from suffering and grief.
column5: Sorrow is also different from suffering and mourning.

column4: Suffering is the endurance of pain-physical, emotional, mental, or spiritual-especially when prolonged or intense.
column5: Suffering is the endurance of pain—physical, emotional, mental, or spiritual—especially when it is prolonged or severe.

column4: Grief is a multifaceted emotional response to significant personal loss, especially relational or existential.
column5: Mourning is a multifaceted emotional response to a significant personal loss, especially of a relationship or of presence.

column4: Sorrow, suffering, and grief are closely related ideas. In the human condition we will experience all three, we can learn and grow through all three, but God will not bring about death and destruction in our lives to teach us.
column5: Grief, suffering, and sorrow are closely related concepts. In the human condition we will go through all three, we can learn and grow through all three, but God will not bring death and destruction into our lives to teach us.

column4: The scriptures say every good and perfect gift is from God above (James 1:17). He is a good Father who knows how to give good gifts to His children (Matthew 7:11). Godly sorrow will cause discomfort, but His discipline is just and loving. Just as a good father would not intentionally break his child’s arm to ‘teach him a lesson’, God will not inflict sickness or disease on His children to teach us.

Godly sorrow will bring discomfort, but His discipline is righteous and loving. column4: ### Example of Worldly Sorrow vs Godly Sorrow
column5: ### An Example of Worldly Sorrow versus Godly Sorrow

column4: A three-year-old boy was playing in the yard with his two-year-old sister. He was playing with a stick, and he intentionally hit her, causing her to cry and leaving a red mark.
column5: A three-year-old boy was playing in the yard with his two-year-old sister. He was playing with a stick, and deliberately hit her, causing her to cry and leaving her with a red mark.

column4: Their father hearing the commotion investigated and when he learned what his son did took the stick, broke it in half and tossed it away. He sent his son inside to think about what did and comforted his daughter.
column5: When their father heard the commotion he investigated, and when he learned what his son had done he took the stick, broke it in two and threw it away. He sent his son inside to think about what he had done and calmed his daughter.

column4: The father coming inside to deal with his son found him crying. Asking him why he was crying his son said, “because you broke my stick”.
column5: When the father came inside to deal with his son he found him crying. When he asked him why he was crying his son said, “because you broke my stick”.

column4: The father’s reply was, “I’m sad that you are more concerned about your stick than you are about your sister who you hurt” and sent him back to his room for more reflection.
column5: The father's reply was, “I am sorry that you care more about your stick than you care about your sister whom you hurt” then he sent him back to his room for further reflection.

column4: A few minutes later his son came back out and apologized. He said he was still sad because dad has broken his stick, and because he had hit his sister.
column5: After a few minutes his son came out again and asked for forgiveness. He said he was still sad because his father had broken his stick, and because he had hit his sister.

column4: **Progress!**
column5: **Progress!**

column4: In this example the boy experienced both worldly sorrow, for his lost stick, and then eventually godly sorrow, for his hurt sister.
column5: In this example the boy experienced worldly sorrow, for the stick he had lost, and then finally godly sorrow, for his sister who had been hurt.

column4: Godly sorrow and God’s goodness are connected. God is a good father that will let us experience the consequences of our actions but will still stand beside us as we walk through those consequences.
column5: Godly sorrow and the goodness of God are linked. God is a good Father who will allow us to go through the consequences of our actions but will still stand by our side as we walk through those consequences.

column4: God's unrelenting goodness, to be willing to redeem us and restore us if we come to Him is a positive agent in our path of repentance. His goodness isn’t that we continue in sin, but that despite our sin He makes a way for us to be redeemed and experience His salvation.
column5: The unending goodness of God, of being ready to redeem us and restore us when we come to Him, is a positive catalyst on our path of repentance. His goodness is not that we should continue in sin, but that despite our sins He makes a way for us to be redeemed and to receive His salvation.

column4: **Romans 2:4** (NKJV) *Or do you despise the riches of His goodness, forbearance, and longsuffering, not knowing that the goodness of God leads you to repentance?*

column4: Despite God’s goodness, mercy, and grace, some people do not repent and do not change, they get stuck in a cycle of frustration and pain. In the extreme opposite, for some people the mere example of sin and consequence in someone else’s life is enough to cause them to change their thinking.
column5: Despite the goodness, mercy, and grace of God, some people do not repent nor change, they get stuck in a cycle of discouragement and pain. On the complete opposite end, for some people just the example of sin and its consequences in another person's life is enough to make them change their minds.

column4: Man has great capacity to change; it's wired into our very essence. Humans are very adaptable, we can learn and grow, and find better ways to do things. However, a capacity to change is not the same as a willingness or a persuasion to change.

column4: I do not know why some people get stuck and others are so ready to change, but I can say that the entire process of change is really from God’s grace.
column5: I do not know why some people get stuck and others are very ready to change, but I can say that the entire process of change is due to the grace of God.

column4: The process of repentance begins before we accept Jesus as our personal Lord and Savior, but the lifestyle of repentance is to endure for our entire Christian walk. We are to throw off dead works and change our minds away from them to the truth of God.
column5: The process of repentance begins before we receive Jesus as our personal Lord and Savior, but the lifestyle of repentance should continue throughout our entire Christian walk. We should cast aside dead works and change our minds from those toward the truth of God.

column4: Repentance can be a purely natural process, but repentance is also the work of the Spirit calling out to us, opening our eyes to the truth, changing our hearts, beckoning us to be transformed. Galatians 6:1 reminds us that some will be ‘stuck’ in a trespass (sin) and need help to get unstuck! That help comes in the form of mature men and women who help restore us in a spirit of gentleness.

column4: The Holy Spirit is the greatest agent for change mankind can engage with, and this is backed up by both the scriptures and by research. Research by “Lyons et al. (2010) found that up to 82% of clients who experienced a spiritual awakening during substance abuse treatment and recovery were completely abstinent at a 1-year follow-up compared with 55% of non-spiritually awakened clients.” \\[2\\] While man can initiate and mediate change, we can accomplish so much more when we walk with God’s Spirit.
column5: The Holy Spirit is the primary agent of change with whom human beings can cooperate, and this is affirmed by Scripture and also by research. A study by “Lyons et al. (2010) found that up to 82% of clients who experienced a spiritual awakening during substance abuse treatment and recovery were completely abstinent at a 1-year follow-up compared with 55% of non-spiritually awakened clients.” [2] While a human being can initiate and lead change, we can accomplish much more when we walk with the Spirit of God.

column4: ### David’s Example of Repentance
column5: ### David’s Model of Repentance

column4: Perhaps no account in the scriptures has a richer example of repentance than the story of King David’s sin found in 2 Samuel 11-12. It begins with King David remaining in Jerusalem instead of going to battle, where he sees Bathsheba bathing. Despite knowing she is the wife of Uriah, one of his loyal soldiers, David sends for her, and they have an affair, resulting in Bathsheba's pregnancy.
column5: Perhaps no narrative in Scripture presents a richer example of repentance than the story of King David’s sin found in 2 Samuel 11-12. It begins with King David remaining in Jerusalem instead of going to war, where he sees Bathsheba bathing. Despite knowing that she was the wife of Uriah, one of his faithful soldiers, David sent for her, and they entered into an adulterous relationship, resulting in Bathsheba becoming pregnant.

column4: To cover his actions, David recalls Uriah from the battlefield, hoping he will spend time with Bathsheba and appear to be the child's father. However, Uriah, out of loyalty to his fellow soldiers, refuses to go to his home with Bethsheba. David then arranges for Uriah to be sent to the front lines where he is ultimately killed in battle. After Uriah's death, David hastily marries Bathsheba to cover up the pregnancy.
column5: To conceal his actions, David brought Uriah back from the battlefield, hoping he would stay with Bathsheba so it would appear that he was the father of the child. However, Uriah, out of loyalty to his fellow soldiers, refused to go to his home to be with Bathsheba. David then arranged for Uriah to be sent to the front lines where he was ultimately killed in battle. After Uriah’s death, David quickly married Bathsheba to hide the pregnancy.

column4: The Lord is displeased with David's actions and sends the prophet Nathan to confront him. When confronted by the prophet, David immediately admitted, "*I have sinned against the Lord*" (2 Samuel 12:13). David did not try to justify or excuse his actions. This confession was the first step in his repentance, acknowledging his wrongdoing directly to God.
column5: The Lord was not pleased with David’s actions and sent the prophet Nathan to confront him. When confronted by the prophet, David immediately confessed, “*I have sinned against the Lord*” (2 Samuel 12:13). David did not try to justify or make excuses for his actions. This confession was the first step in his repentance, acknowledging his wrongdoing directly to God.

column4: In Psalm 51, David’s words, “*For I know my transgressions, and my sin is always before me,*” show his complete ownership of his actions. He expresses grief not only for the sin itself but also for how it offended God, saying, “*Against you, you only, have I sinned.*” David displayed "*a broken and contrite heart,*" an essential part of true repentance (Psalm 51:17). This sorrow wasn’t superficial; he deeply grieved over the sin he committed and the hurt it caused. This depth of remorse was a sign that he wanted not only forgiveness but a changed heart.
column5: In Psalm 51, David’s words, “*For I know my transgressions, and my sin is always before me,*” show his complete ownership of his actions. He shows sorrow not only for the sin itself but also for how it offended God, saying, “*Against you, you only, have I sinned.*” David displayed “*a broken and contrite heart,*” a vital part of true repentance (Psalm 51:17). This sorrow was not superficial; he mourned deeply over the sin he committed and the pain it caused. This depth of regret was a sign that he desired not only forgiveness but also a transformed heart.

column4: David asked God to “*Create in me a pure heart, O God, and renew a steadfast spirit within me”* (Psalm 51:10). He sought an inner transformation that would prevent him from repeating the same mistakes. Rather than just apologizing, David pleaded with God to cleanse him, saying, “*Wash me, and I will be whiter than snow*” (Psalm 51:7). He recognized that only God could purify his heart and restore his joy.
column5: David asked God, “*Create in me a clean heart, O God, and renew a steadfast spirit within me*” (Psalm 51:10). He wanted an inner change that would prevent him from repeating the same mistakes. Rather than asking only for forgiveness, David cried out for God to cleanse him, saying, “*Wash me, and I shall be whiter than snow*” (Psalm 51:7). He recognized that only God could purify his heart and restore his joy.

column4: David’s desire to be renewed spiritually reflects a genuine commitment to walk in God’s ways moving forward. His request for a “*willing spirit*” (Psalm 51:12) demonstrates his hope to be aligned with God in every part of his life.
column5: David’s desire to be renewed spiritually shows a true commitment to walk in God’s ways going forward. His request for a “*willing spirit*” (Psalm 51:12) reflects his hope of being reconciled to God in every part of his life.

column4: Although God put away David’s sin, the Lord struck the child and he was very sick. David fasted, prayed, and pleaded with God to spare the child, but when the child died, David accepted it (2 Samuel 12:15-23).
column5: Although God put away David’s sin, the Lord struck the child and he became very ill. David fasted, prayed, and begged God to spare the child, but when the child died, David accepted it (2 Samuel 12:15-23).

column4: In Psalm 51 we find a personal prayer of repentance and a public acknowledgment of his transgressions. David’s decision to write down his plea for mercy, creating one of the Bible’s most enduring psalms, shows his willingness to be transparent about his sin and God’s forgiveness. This psalm became a testimony of repentance and restoration for others to learn from, memorializing his journey from guilt to grace.
column5: In Psalm 51 we find a personal prayer of repentance and an open confession of his wrongdoing. David’s decision to write his plea for mercy, forming one of the most enduring psalms in the Bible, shows his willingness to be open about his sin and God’s forgiveness. This psalm became a testimony of repentance and restoration for others to learn from, recording his journey from guilt to grace.

column4: David’s repentance journey was not simply about feeling sorry; it was a profound change in his heart and life. Through confession, acceptance, and the heart transformation inscribed in Psalm 51, David memorialized his sin as a lesson on God’s mercy, repentance, and the possibility of restoration, making his story one of the Bible's most significant examples of genuine repentance.
column5: David’s journey of repentance was not just about feeling remorse; it was a deep transformation in his heart and life. Through the confession, acceptance, and heart change recorded in Psalm 51, David memorialized his sin as a lesson about God’s mercy, repentance, and the possibility of restoration, making his story among the most important examples of true repentance in the Bible.
